CausalChain: Chronic liver inflammation (HBV/HCV/cirrhosis) -> Elevated inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α) -> Upregulation of specific glycosyltransferases (FUT8, ST6GAL1) -> Aberrant glycosylation of AFP -> Increased conversion to AFP-L3 -> AFP-L3 engages oncogenic signaling (STAT3, NF-κB) & transcriptional networks -> Aggressive tumor behavior (vascular invasion, poor differentiation) -> Worsened prognosis in HCC
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in the setting of chronic liver inflammation, elevated levels of IL-6 and TNF-α selectively induce the expression of glycosyltransferases such as FUT8 and ST6GAL1 in hepatocytes. This cytokine-mediated enzymatic upregulation leads to a distinctive pattern of AFP glycosylation, resulting in a pronounced increase in the formation of the AFP-L3 isoform. Beyond its traditional role as a diagnostic marker, AFP-L3 is proposed to participate directly in HCC pathogenesis by modulating oncogenic signaling pathways—including STAT3 and NF-κB—as well as liver-specific transcription factors. These interactions foster tumor aggressiveness, exemplified by augmented vascular invasion and poor cellular differentiation. By implementing CRISPR-mediated gene editing to modulate expression of implicated glycosyltransferases, combined with single-cell transcriptomic profiling and high-resolution glycomics, we aim to delineate this mechanistic cascade and explore its application as a dual diagnostic and therapeutic target in HCC.
Abstract: Chronic liver inflammation, as seen in conditions such as HBV, HCV, and cirrhosis, leads to a pro-inflammatory cytokine milieu dominated by IL-6 and TNF-α. We hypothesize that these cytokines specifically upregulate discrete glycosyltransferases—most notably FUT8 and ST6GAL1—in hepatocytes. The resulting enzymatic shift drives aberrant glycosylation of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), preferentially generating the AFP-L3 isoform. Far from serving solely as a biomarker, AFP-L3 is proposed to actively engage with and modulate oncogenic signaling pathways such as STAT3 and NF-κB, as well as key liver-specific transcription factor networks. This interaction is predicted to facilitate aggressive tumor phenotypes, characterized by increased vascular invasion and poor cellular differentiation, ultimately worsening the prognosis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Our study leverages contemporary molecular tools—including CRISPR-based gene editing, single-cell transcriptomics, and high-resolution glycomics—to dissect this cytokine–glycosyltransferase–AFP-L3 axis and evaluate its diagnostic and therapeutic potential.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis retains the original causal framework—chronic inflammation leading to cytokine elevation, glycosyltransferase upregulation, altered AFP glycosylation, and subsequent activation of oncogenic signaling—while addressing the review comments by specifying the key enzymes (FUT8, ST6GAL1) and elucidating potential signaling mediators (STAT3, NF-κB). The new version strengthens the mechanistic link between AFP-L3 and tumor aggressiveness, and incorporates contemporary molecular tools such as CRISPR, single-cell transcriptomics, and high-resolution glycomics to detail experimental validation strategies, thereby enhancing both the novelty and practical implementability of the hypothesis.
